sections.heading: Looking back on your care this week
sections.text: Father, another week is ending, and I can see that I have not carried myself through it. You have kept me in the ordinary movements of my life—leaving home, coming back, working, resting, meeting people, making decisions. There were dangers I noticed and dangers I never saw, and you were watching over me in both. Thank you for protecting me, providing for me, and holding my life in your hands hour by hour.
theological_themes: God’s preserving care through ordinary life
Providence over seen and unseen dangers

scripture_references.connection: This psalm speaks of the Lord keeping his people in the whole course of life, not only in dramatic crises. It supports the prayer’s gratitude for God’s watchful care in daily going and returning.
James grounds every good gift in God’s generous character. That fits the prayer’s recognition that provision, safety, and comfort are not self-produced achievements but gifts from the Father.

sections.heading: Receiving your gifts without making them my home
sections.text: You have fed me, comforted me, and given me more kindness than I deserved. You have given me relationships and friends that have brought real joy. You have also given me your Word and the ordinary helps that strengthen faith, and through them you have reminded me that this world is not my final rest. Even when life goes well, keep bringing me back to what matters most: that I would love my Savior, listen to him, and belong to him above everything else.
theological_themes: Scripture and means of grace as spiritual nourishment
Earthly blessings are not ultimate rest

scripture_references.connection: Hebrews teaches believers not to treat the present world as their lasting city. This supports the prayer’s movement from enjoying God’s gifts to remembering that final rest is still ahead.
Jesus tells Martha that one thing is necessary as Mary sits at his feet. The prayer echoes that priority: even amid many good things, devotion to Christ must remain central.
Paul describes Scripture as God-given and useful for shaping and equipping God’s people. This grounds the prayer’s thanks for the Book that instructs and corrects the believer’s desires.

sections.heading: Confessing what your kindness exposes
sections.text: Lord, your mercies are more than I can count—and my sins and failures are painfully many too. I do not want to hide them from you, explain them away, or make them sound smaller than they are. You have been faithful and generous to me, and I have still been slow to love, quick to wander, half-hearted in obedience, and careless with time and grace. I come to you honestly, with a humbled heart.
theological_themes: Sin seen in the light of God’s mercy

scripture_references.connection: John warns against denying sin and calls believers to confess it before the faithful and just God. This directly supports the prayer’s refusal to conceal or minimize sin.
David’s repentance shows that God receives a contrite heart rather than outward religious performance used to cover sin. This illuminates the prayer’s desire to confess with true brokenness.

sections.heading: Resting in the forgiveness Jesus bought
sections.text: If I had to review my life in secret with no mercy to turn to, I would be undone. But you are not reluctant to forgive. With you there is deep redemption, real pardon, and mercy that teaches me to fear you with reverence instead of running from you in despair. So I put my hope in the blood of Jesus, shed on the cross for sinners like me. Let his sacrifice be my confidence tonight.
theological_themes: Assurance grounded in God’s forgiving mercy
Reverent fear produced by forgiveness, not despair

scripture_references.connection: The psalmist admits that no one could stand if God marked iniquities, yet finds hope because forgiveness belongs to God. This closely matches the prayer’s movement from self-examination to reverent confidence in mercy.
The same psalm speaks of plentiful redemption with the Lord and his power to redeem from iniquity. It supports the prayer’s trust that God’s mercy is abundant enough for real guilt.
Paul locates redemption and forgiveness in Christ’s blood and in the riches of God’s grace. This grounds the prayer’s confidence not in emotional sincerity but in the cross.

sections.heading: Asking to live wisely before the end
sections.text: As I look toward a new week, do more in me than forgive me. Dress me in humility. Wake me up where I have grown dull. Make me more devoted to you in the actual choices of my days. Keep the end of my life in view—not to make me anxious, but to make me wise. Cure me of putting off obedience, drifting in indecision, and acting as if I have endless time. Teach me how fragile I am, help me number my days, and give me a heart that lives wisely before you.
theological_themes: Mortality as a call to wisdom

scripture_references.connection: Moses asks God to teach his people to number their days so that they may gain wisdom. This directly supports the prayer’s request to live in light of mortality rather than waste time.
Paul urges believers to wake from spiritual sleep and live in the light because the time is short. This fits the prayer’s plea to be quickened, decisive, and more devoted to God.

Paul calls those who belong to Christ to put on humility and live a whole-life obedience shaped by Christ’s peace and word. This supports the prayer’s request to be clothed with humility and changed in daily practice.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original phrase “means of grace” comes from a Reformed devotional context. I rendered it as “the ordinary helps that strengthen faith” while preserving the idea that God uses Word and worship to build up believers.

The phrase about comforts that “indulged” the speaker could be misunderstood today as sinful self-indulgence. I treated it as lawful creaturely comfort received from God, not as permission for excess.
The original’s statement that “this is not my rest” could sound like contempt for creation if isolated. I framed it as gratitude for earthly gifts while refusing to treat them as ultimate.
The line “that thou mayest be feared” is rooted in Psalm 130, where forgiveness produces reverent fear. I clarified that this is not despairing terror but worshipful reverence before a merciful God.
significant_interpretive_choices: I interpreted the prayer as an end-of-week Lord’s Day evening reflection: looking back on preservation and grace, confessing sin, resting in redemption, and asking for wiser obedience in the week ahead.
I treated “secret reviews of my life” as honest self-examination before God, not morbid introspection detached from gospel assurance.
I kept the original’s progression from thanksgiving to confession to assurance to sanctification, rather than turning it into a general evening prayer.
I rendered “to be quickened in thy way” as being awakened where dull and made more alive in obedience, preserving the older sense of spiritual enlivening.
